utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. The Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey alone. From the Defence teams, it's only Mr. Meek who is absent. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Judges. I would like to take this opportunity to introduce a new legal assistant on our team, Ms. [indiscernible] from France. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, bonjour and welcome to you. Mr. Butler, welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madame Fauveau is going to cross-examine you today. Madame Fauveau, what's your estimate? And good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, eight hours, but of course I'll do my best to complete my cross-examination earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's start. I would suggest so, because the longer this evidence takes, the more counterproductive it can become.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic. I represent General Miletic. On the 15th of January, you mentioned the humanitarian convoys, and you said that your task was not to provide a comprehensive view on the policy regarding humanitarian convoys. I would like, however, to ask you whether you conducted an analysis concerning the period going from March to July 1995 regarding the number of convoys that were announced and the number of convoys that were refused access.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Throughout the same period, you did not, did you, conduct an analysis about the number of convoys that were authorised access but that, for another reason, never went to the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am, I did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 15th of January, you stated that the policy of the staff of the VRS, in terms of the convoys, was directly linked to directive number 7. Did you conduct an analysis of the policy of the Republika Srpska and its army regarding the convoys before the directive was passed; in other words, before March 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In that case, how can you say that the policy of the Army of the Republika Srpska, in relation to the convoys, was linked to directive number 7? How can you state that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, it's pretty self-evident in directive 7 what that policy is, so all I did at that juncture was then look at the convoy documents to determine whether or not there was evidence that such policies were being carried out. Now, with respect to the Dutch Battalion and their effect in January and February and March, prior to that, I believe their testimony doesn't reflect the fact that their soldiers were not being permitted back into the enclaves or that they were not being seriously degraded in their -- the supplies that they were getting until approximately the March 1995 time frame. So, granted, while I did not take into account a statistical analysis of that, I did do it on a more anecdotal basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that you do not know whether the percentage [Realtime transcript read in error, "personage"] of convoys that were refused after the directive was higher than before the directive? "Percentage." I was talking about percentage, and I see in the transcript that the word "personage" has been included.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, you're correct, I cannot give you a statistical breakdown.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that the policy of Republika Srpska and the policy of its army was the result of the abuse made of the convoys because weapons had been transported in these convoys, as well as humanitarian aid for the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. For the convoys, Bosnia-wide in general, the VRS was aware of situations where weapons and other illicit goods were being smuggled in on US -- UN vehicles, I should say, so certainly that is a consideration that the VRS would have taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know that the procedure regarding to the authorisation for humanitarian aid convoys was different from the procedure regarding UNPROFOR convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Are you aware that orders related to humanitarian aid convoys existed right at the beginning of the war and that the procedure did not change, was not modified, after the directive was passed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that as a fact, so I'm just not familiar with convoy operations in the early war years, so I can't tell you "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like Exhibit 5D605 to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the meantime, I'll tell you that it's an order from the VRS Main Staff, from the 31st of August, 1994, regarding the movement of humanitarian aid. Please turn to paragraph 1 of this order. At paragraphs 1 and 2, it appears that authorisations were delivered by the coordination organ. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This appears to be a two-page -- if could can see the whole order before he's asked questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Yes, yes, I think he can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'm reading it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was: There's a whole another part to this. This may be an order, but the foregoing, you know, he ought to be able to look at as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Madam Registrar heard that too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Am I on page 1 or -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise, we get a hard copy and give it to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 2, please. Thank you. Okay, ma'am, if you could ask your question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we turn back to page 1 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My question is the following: Would you agree that with respect to paragraphs 1 and 2 of this order, approvals regarding humanitarian convoys were issued by the coordinating body?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, they were the initial approval authority, but as you can tell from the remainder of the body of the order, the fact that they would initially approve a convoy, the Main Staff made it quite clear, in the body of the order, that if it wasn't coordinated through them, it still wasn't going through.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But if you turn to paragraph 4 on this first page of the document, we can see that the document says sent by the VRS Main Staff to its subordinate units, was a notification, notification regarding the convoys that had been approved and the convoys that had not been approved?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it's saying, at least to my reading, ma'am, is that they're complaining that one of the problems that they have is that even though convoys may have been approved by the coordinating body, they're aware that sometimes they're not getting notified and that these convoys are showing up unannounced at VRS check-points and it's causing a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I don't want to argue with you. At paragraph 3 on this same page, mention is made of the control of the VRS on the movement of convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. It specifically states that the army has the obligation to check the teams and convoys passing through the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now turn to page 2 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At point 1 of this order, convoys that had not been announced were not allowed to go through?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, it's what it's saying, is that unless they receive -- unless the subordinate formations receive authorisation in writing from the Main Staff, they're not to permit the convoy to pass.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the remaining parts of this order, we have a list of the controls that subordinated formations or units are supposed to conduct when a convoy appears?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that these measures are precisely the same as the one that existed in 1995, provided of course that you know what measures were to be followed in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, ma'am, with respect to the technical goods and humanitarian aid issues, it just seems to be the same type of order. The fact that they're not to allow anything more that pass -- that's been authorised to pass, anything else will be confiscated, so in that sense it's correct. This order obviously does not regulate anything with respect to the issue of UN or even international personnel who leave a particular area and what the policy is on allowing them to return, so in that respect it is different.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This order indeed only mentions humanitarian convoys. Now I'd like to ask you a question about UNPROFOR convoys. Do you know that the VRS had concluded several agreements regarding UNPROFOR convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I am aware that the VRS did deal with the UN on the issue of their particular convoys. I don't know the technical details of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to see the agreements passed between the VRS and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For which particular time frame, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: 1995, and especially after the directive was passed.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I don't believe I've seen any agreements or any of the technical agreements with the UN with respect to those convoys for post-March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But before March 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe my association with those documents relates to convoys passing between the VRS positions around Sarajevo. They're not directly related to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D725, please. It's not been translated. I hope that the Prosecutor will not ask me to read the entire document. It's an agreement between UNPROFOR and the VRS from 12th July 1995. My questions regarding these -- this document are of a technical nature. I don't believe that the substance of the document matters so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: First of all, have you had the document to --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document says 12th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document says "12 Feb," sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sure Madame Fauveau will come up with an alternative for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is 12 February 1995. I might have misspoken. But in any case, it's the 12th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to see this document before? It's a document related to the movement of UNPROFOR on the VRS territory.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ma'am, if it hasn't been translated, even if I did see it, I wouldn't be able to really process it, so I guess the answer is "no."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to process this document, but this document is related to an agreement between the VRS and the UNPROFOR on the 31st of January, 1995. At paragraph 2, we see the name of Zdravko Tolimir. He's the one who signed the agreement on behalf of the VRS. Would you have any idea about why the VRS decided that Zdravko Tolimir would be the one to sign this agreement related to the movement of UNPROFOR on the territory?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from my previous work in other cases that General Tolimir was frequently one of the individuals who dealt with the UNPROFOR people on a higher level. So it wouldn't surprise me that he would be the person that the VRS had dealing with the UN as a way of concluding this agreement. So, I mean, to me it's not -- it's not remarkable that he is. He has had many prior high-level dealings with the UN in the past, so that doesn't surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D727. It's in English. Could we see the signature at the bottom of the document. It's a letter sent by General Ratko Mladic to General Bernard Janvier. If you turn to the text itself of the document, you'll see that reference is made to an agreement passed on the 4th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to see this agreement of 4th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe so, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This document mentions contacts between the liaison officers in the enclaves with the local commanders of UNPROFOR. Have you had access to the material related to these contacts that apparently took place on the 6th of June, 1995, if we are to believe this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am. With respect to Srebrenica, and Zepa, for that matter, I am not aware of any meeting notes or things of that nature that -- that would have occurred on 6 June 1995. It certainly may very well have happened, but I don't recall coming across any notes reflecting that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like the witness to be shown Exhibit 5D615.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And whilst it's being displayed, can you tell me what was the role of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska in relation to the movement of convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not particularly aware that other than issues related to -- I mean, particularly with the UN convoys, the military convoys, I'm not aware that they had any role outside of issues of the check -- you know, the joint manning of check-points and traffic control to ensure that the convoy didn't go off route. I don't know what role they played in the issues related to the other humanitarian convoys, the ICRC, the food convoys and things of that nature. I would have assumed they'd provide the same role, route security and things of that nature. I don't know that they were in the approval process, per se, in the same way that the Main Staff was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This document is dated the 13th of March, 1995, and we can read, right at the beginning of the document, it's a document from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska, sent to the Public Security Centre of Bijeljina, Zvornik and Sarajevo. And at the beginning of the document, we can read the following: [In English] "We are hereby informing you that the movement of representative of the ICRC has been approved, so that you can take measures accordingly. "Tuesday, 14 March 1995 - the coordination body for humanitarian aid number 383-ICRC-255." [Interpretation] According to this document, the Ministry for the interior did have to take a number of measures, particularly when reference is made to a convoy and reference is made to the coordination body. Do you agree that in this particular case the coordination body had approved the convoy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, it says it's been approved. I assume it's from the coordination body. But I think as you can also tell from the header information, I mean, it appears that the primary reason for this is the -- is to notify the border crossing station that these people would be arriving, as well as part of their route. And certainly the physical control of the international border would have been a MUP responsibility, not an army one in this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would then like to show you document P2522. It's a document that you analysed on the 15th of January last. It was signed by the Colonel Miletic at the time, General Miletic. Now, if you look at the bottom of the first page in the English version, this document refers to another document which is dated the 6th of March, 1995 as well and in which the approved convoys are listed. Did you ever see this other document with the approved convoys? Document 0618102.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ma'am, I looked at the entire suite of documents, so it's entirely possible that I did see the approved convoy document, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go on to page 3 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We can see that on the 6th of March, it was at 2200 hours. Do you see the time and the date on the document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let me now show you the document P5D620. This is the document I just -- well, the previous document just referred to, in other words, the staff document 0618102. This is document 5D620. Can we now look at the last page of this document -- or rather page 3 first. Page 3 in the English version, please. The bottom of the page, please. Lower down, please. I want to take a look at the name. Sir, this document was written, at least from what we see here, the General Milovanovic is apparent here on this document. Now let me show you the last page. I'd like to see the seal. On the seal, what we see is "6th of March, 2030" or "2045." How can you explain that General Milovanovic -- well, that his name is on this document which came out at 2035 and that two hours later Colonel Miletic's name appears on the -- another document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain that. He could either be physically there or it's just that is the way that they -- you know, they either -- they chose to put it that way. I mean, I have no explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we come back to P2522, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the meantime, you said, on the 15th of January last, that when General Miletic, who was a colonel at the time, sent out this document, he gave instructions whereby the subordinate units had to -- well, that the subordinate units had to comply with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: ... And that in the absence of the notification, in any case, the convoys would not have been able to go through?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your question must have been mistranslated. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that in the absence of such a notification, in any case, no convoy would have been able to go through?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I mean, the General Staff -- sorry, the Main Staff, you know, had made it clear that unless the units who were manning the check-points at various locations had received a written clearance message that they were not to permit any of the convoys through, so I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So this, in itself, doesn't change anything? The fate of the convoys is exactly the same, with or without this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document, the one signed by General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: No, this one that gives the list of the convoys that are not approved.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am. The list of the -- the document -- the convoys that it's not approved is an additional backstop so that the VRS people at the check-points, if a particular convoy showed up without explanation, there would be some awareness of it and the soldiers would know and the officers there would know specifically to turn it around. The reason behind doing that was to prevent, you know, an individual from essentially talking their way through a check-point by saying that clearance has been granted and that it must be just a paperwork issue or something like that. This way, the VRS people had explicit instructions as to which convoys were permitted to pass and under what circumstance, and they also had the list of which convoys were not permitted to pass under any circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, but you do agree that on the notification -- according to the notification, the convoys could not go through?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first part of this document, at least the one I'm looking at here, it talks about "informing you of the convoys that were approved." Now, like I said, at part of these things, they also -- on each of these same orders, they also did list which convoys were not approved, and I think if you scroll down on this one, you'll see the notation to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I show the witness my copy. This is the paper copy of the same document, to make things easier, but before looking at this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Before that: You said, on the 15th of January, last page 19716, that this particular document said the following: [In English] "We at the Main Staff have already decided that these convoys will not pass. We are informing you of our decision. In the event that the convoy shows up at the check-point and is one of these convoys that has already been denied, you are to take the following measures."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. And as you note right here, on page 2 of the English translations, it goes into that exact thing that I've just discussed. It tells you about which convoys were approved, and then it tells you, and just in case, so there's no confusion here, the ones that were not approved and why. So, you know, this particular order does discuss that. It discusses which ones were not approved.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My question is slightly different. When you said that this document said "we at the staff have not approved the following convoys," can you take a look at the document, please? Would you agree to say that the document in no place says either -- either "we" or "the General Staff of the Republika Srpska," all it says is that these convoys are not approved?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, it may be a linguistic issue, but the way the first sentence reads in English, it says, you know: "In order to exercise strict control over the movement of convoys and teams which alone have been approved, we hereby provide details of the convoys which have not been approved." So given the fact that the order is from the Main Staff, you know, I take it that -- from that that these are the ones that the Main Staff did not approve. Now, I could stand to be corrected, in that these were not approved at the commission level, but that's not how I read the document. And, again, it may very well be a linguistics issue and not a factual one.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In any case, I do not dispute that this document says that the convoys are not approved, but it doesn't spell out who did that. And on the basis of this document alone, one cannot exclude that the coordination body may have not approved that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, that is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were in the witness box on the 15th of January, you talked about Bratunac and the Bratunac Brigade. It's document P230 we're talking about. This document dealt with the situation in the Bratunac Brigade from the 1st of January to the 30th of June, 1995, and in this document it is written that the check-point was established for the purpose of monitoring entries and exits from and into Srebrenica. What I would like to know is whether you are in agreement with the fact that this check-point referred to was indeed established well before the 1st of January, 1995.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. As far as I'm aware, the yellow bridge check-point, as its referred to, existed from at least late 1993 onwards. It was the primary road in and out. They did not allow convoys to enter through the back way into Srebrenica, which would be the Zeleni Jadar road. So everything went over the yellow bridge, so far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We agree, then, that this check-point was not established as a consequence of directive number 7?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D321.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And whilst the document is being displayed, I would like to say that it's a Zvornik Brigade document that you were shown, and it deals with a number of goods that were confiscated from MSF. Could page 2 in English be shown, point 10 in particular. You've analysed two of the reports from the Zvornik Brigade which stated that sometimes goods would be confiscated from convoys. Did you review the entire collection of the Zvornik Brigade documents dealing with the convoys that went through that territory?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I mean, I would have read the reports, but I don't believe I looked at them from the context of -- of the convoy issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Don't you think that for the period from March and -- between -- to July 1995, it would have been relevant to find out how many convoys went through without any problems instead of focusing on just two convoys that had difficulties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The goal in this context was -- and again looking at 7-1, and primarily not with respect to the humanitarian good convoys, but for my purpose the key thing was the convoys that were being permitted to leave the enclave with UN personnel and not being permitted to return with those same personnel, again as part of the larger plan of adversely impacting the ability of the UN to perform its mission, which was something within the larger goal of the VRS. It wasn't to do, as I've indicated before, a broad statistical analysis of the convoys back and forth through there and come up with a comprehensive list of materials as to what was permitted to pass and what wasn't. I mean, I agree that it is -- you know, in this case, you know, it is illustrative in nature. It's not meant to be a comprehensive convoy review, and I don't believe I've ever said that it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that when a convoy showed up at a check-point, it was supposed to have all relevant documents listing the goods transported and the quantity of goods in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, that is correct. They were -- the VRS required them to have everything completely manifested.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if the goods confiscated in this convoy was not listed in the documents or if the quantity listed was not the same as the one in the convoy, then the goods should have been confiscated, according to the rules of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. As we earlier discussed, and I believe you actually had that particular order up, the units were told by the Main Staff that they were to confiscate anything that was beyond the listed authorised item.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade properly reported to the Drina Corps that the goods had been confiscated; that's what happened?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, they listed as part of their daily combat report the goods that they had confiscated. I did not try and cross-index this to a convoy -- to a particular convoy listing to find out whether or not these goods were above what was manifested or not. I mean, I don't know that we even have that information that would reflect whether or not the goods in this convoy were properly listed or not, so I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Drina Corps reported to the Main Staff that these goods had been confiscated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the first page of the document displayed on screen, the first page of this Zvornik Brigade report. It's a report dated April 4th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D722 now. It's a Drina Corps Command report dated the 4th of April, 1995. Unfortunately, this document has not been translated into English. I read out the relevant part in B/C/S. I know -- I think that you are familiar with regular combat reports from this brigade or from the corps. We can see what's the situation on -- in the area of responsibility. "Situation under control. All the planned convoys and UNPROFOR teams have passed through our territory without any delays." Would you agree that under these circumstances, or here in particular, the Drina Corps has not correctly reported the situation to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this context, it's clear that the Drina Corps did not feel that it needed to notify the Main Staff of whatever confiscated material there was. All it noted was that the convoys had passed as scheduled. So I agree with you, there is no accounting of confiscated material.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The goods that were confiscated were confiscated from an MSF convoy. Do you remember that or should I show you the exhibit again?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know that before April 1995, there had been problems with MSF?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? I mean, that's a pretty broad -- what type of problems are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know that Medecins Sans Frontieres, MSF, brought an unauthorised goods into the enclave, they abused the trust of the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that there were reports of MSF trying to bring in additional medical and other related gear in excess to what was often manifested, so I guess if that's what you mean by "problems," yes, I am aware of that. I just want to make sure we weren't getting into a situation like the UN, where there were allegations of fuel and weapons. I'm not aware of any of those allegations against MSF.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you Exhibit 5D609. It's a report by Momir Nikolic. It's a report from the intelligence organ of the Bratunac Brigade, dated January 11th, 1995. I'd like you to turn to the penultimate paragraph on the first page in English. In this paragraph, we can read: [In English] "I would also like to inform you that the coordinator of the MSF, Medecins Sans Frontieres organisation, publicly apologized for the abuse of trust of one of his members in Srebrenica and publicly admitted that the Serbian side has behaved perfectly correctly when it confiscated the vehicle and smuggled goods. This delegate, Jean, was removed from the MFS organisation and returned to his country because of abuse of trust and smuggling with Muslims from Srebrenica and Naser Oric." [Interpretation] Have you had the opportunity to read this report before?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could he be allowed to read the entire document? Again, we're just getting pieces of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are two things. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe I've seen this document before, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then I think you need time to go through it, unless you are going to be very limited in your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was my only question related to this document. The Prosecutor has submitted volumes of documents to the witness whilst only showing fractions of these documents, so I don't mind if the witness is given time to read out this document. But then I will ask for more time for my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: She can count on an objection every time that we're getting piecemeal documents. We've seen the problem with that. These are important matters, and Mr. Butler, as I know the Court knows, needs to see the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But what's your question? Your question is whether he's seen this document before or what?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My question was whether the witness had ever heard of this incident and whether he had seen this document. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think you can answer that, Mr. Butler, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. No, I'm not aware of the specific incident in question, and like I said, I don't recall. I might have seen this document at some juncture in the past, but it doesn't stand out as something that -- that I'm remembering. So, I mean, I can't say that as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know that the policy of Republika Srpska and the Army of Republika Srpska was exactly the same concerning the enclaves in Eastern Bosnia compared to the other ones, such as Sarajevo, Tuzla, Bihac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For what periods of time, ma'am, because in July -- in late 1995, that's not necessarily the case. I mean, we know, for example, that when we look at what happened in particularly Srebrenica and Zepa, where the UN was completely dependent upon the VRS for access to the enclaves, that in many cases the UN soldiers were not being allowed to return.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I think we're talking about two quite different things. I'm talking about humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That was an interruption of Mr. Butler in the middle of an answer, and it was a very broad question and he was attempting to answer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let him answer the question first. Mr. Butler, could you proceed with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was it. I believe that the issue was that with respect to the eastern enclaves, that the policy, particularly after directive 7, was different than it was in enclaves such as Sarajevo, Tuzla and Bihac, primarily because in Srebrenica and Zepa, the UN was -- and the International Community was completely dependent upon the VRS for access. They weren't dependent upon the VRS for access, for example, to get to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you analyse the humanitarian convoys that went to Tuzla, Bihac and Sarajevo to find out -- well, to be able to assert that the policy was not the same as compared with Eastern Bosnia, as between the two?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, again I didn't analyse that, and certainly, you know, one of the issues that occurred in the middle of that process that completely threw everything out of kilter was in May of 1995, when the NATO air strikes began, and almost all cross-conflict lines movement stopped because of the VRS, you know, apprehending UN soldiers in that regard. So, I mean, it's tough to do a broad statistical analysis as to what all of that meant, given that that particular event occurred in the middle, which skews everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that what happened concerning the NATO strikes and the impact that this had on the convoys had nothing to do with directive number 7?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I agree. I mean, it did not -- it was not a cause-and-effect relationship to directive number 7, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like now to show you document 5D728. It is a document that is rather lengthy. We received it last Thursday from the -- from the OTP, and hopefully the OTP will not ask us to read it out in full. It is a report on the application of the agreement on the cessation of hostilities, March 1995, and what is of interest to me is on page 4 of this document, point 7, concerning the UNHCR convoy. And we're talking about UNHCR convoys and humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We see in this paragraph that on the 28th of March, 43 of 263 UNHCR planned convoys were blocked, and right at the bottom of the same paragraph we can see that 22.800 metric tons of humanitarian aid was intended for the enclave, but in actual fact 18.000 metric tons arrived. And then we see the proportions for each enclave. We see that Bihac received 29 per cent, Sarajevo 71 per cent, Srebrenica 93 per cent, Zepa 80 per cent, and Gorazde 83 per cent. Now, when we see that the Srebrenica enclave received 71 per cent -- and I grant you that we're talking about March 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 93 per cent, the interpreter corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we really talk about a policy of obstruction?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, as you said it yourself, we're talking about March. I mean, directive 7-1 was just being published, and obviously there's going to be a lag between the actual implementation -- or actual directive and then the actual implementation of it. So, you know, I grant it up to March, it appears that 93 per cent of the aid is being delivered. I don't know that that number is valid for April and beyond.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, I don't know whether you saw the information for the other months. I haven't seen them, so I can't refer to them. But since you are mentioning this, do you know the data concerning the other months, April, May, June?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I don't, and that's why I say, I mean, I don't know that this number is valid, I mean, so there's just -- as far as I know, there is no data with respect to the period April, May, June, until 1 July when everything pretty much stopped at that juncture. So I don't know what the situation is with respect to a number on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go down and let Mr. Butler read a few more paragraphs down to paragraph 12 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. But can he read until paragraph 12 or is it too small? Yeah, it should be okay now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Enough, yeah, okay. Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the OTP would like to take over the cross-examination, but in any case I have no further questions on this particular document. I would like to go on to another document, 5D729.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Before we see this document, can you tell us whether you know that in 1995 -- are you aware of a ceasefire that was signed at the end of 1994 and was valid until the 30th of April, 1995, concerning all of the territory, not just Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I am aware that there was a broader ceasefire in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that during the ceasefire, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina undertook to arm itself considerably?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, they did, and the VRS was well aware of that fact at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The document that you now see, we're talking about a report from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan concerning the attitude of the Bosnian government to UNPROFOR, dated 1st of March, 1995, I'd like to show you a little down on this page, in the middle of the paragraph, there's a sentence that begins: [In English] "Despite the acceptance of the cessation of hostility agreement on 31st December 1994 and of the accords of several joint commissions held at the various command level, the BiH has obstructed attempts by UNPROFOR to improve liaison, observe confrontation lines, and separate forces by refusing to attend regularly the joint commission process. They have applied significant additional restrictions on UNPROFOR movement, increased the tempo of their own force restructuring, resupply and training, and threatened the lives of the BSA liaison officers."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, could Mr. Butler be allowed to look at the whole document? It's hard to say who, where, what this has to do with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this a long document? How many pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Twenty-five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime, can we know what your question is so that more or less --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the witness know about this policy at the beginning of 1995 vis-a-vis the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, with respect to where I obtained my knowledge of that is the review of the United Nations report on Srebrenica which incorporates, you know, many of these same documents. So in that respect, you know, I was aware, and as I believe I just said, I mean, the ABiH did in fact use the ceasefire period in order to militarily strengthen their own capabilities, and part of that was denying the UN, particularly their liaison people, access to some of the BiH military units and front lines, as a way of trying to keep that restructuring and retraining and re-equipping secret. So, I mean, that's a known fact and certainly one that I was aware of, and, as I indicated earlier, one that the VRS was aware of as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we have the break? Can I suggest that we limit our breaks to 20 minutes instead of 25 minutes today so that we will try and recover 10 of the 20 minutes we lost in the beginning because of technical problems. Is it okay? All right, okay. So we'll have a 20-minute break instead of 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened? Did we lose all the previous transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we begin, page 26, line 25, the question was whether the witness knew -- was aware of the policy of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the ABiH, but I do believe that the witness's answer was completely clear. I still need 5D729, document 5D729, page 2 of this document. The same document as we had just before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You can see paragraph 3 of this document: [In English] "The BiH has improved numerous restrictions on movement ROM on UNPROFOR. The historical trend is that the ROM are levied wherever the BiH is undertaking military activity or attempting to pressure UNPROFOR. Over the past two months, the BiH has applied ROM in Sector North East and South West presumably to screen their military activities and also to force the withdrawal of the BSA liaison officers from Tuzla and Gornji Vakuf." My question is: When this document talks about the North East sector, this is indeed where Srebrenica was located, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. From the UN geographical perspective, Srebrenica would be included in United Nations Sector North East.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And then paragraph -- subparagraph (a), at the end of that subparagraph what we see is: [Previous translation continues] [In English] "... In the northern region of the sector as well as UNPROFOR movement in the Zepa town in the west of Srebrenica enclave are the subject of restrictions imposed by the BiH. Concurrently, an unprecedented number of BiH fuel and supply convoys have been seen moving into the northern region of the sector." [Interpretation] What I would like to know: You said, on the 15th of January last, page 19721, that most of the goods that were not authorised to enter into the enclaves, well, these could have been used in one way or another for military needs. Do you think -- do you not think that the policy of the authorities of Republika Srpska concerning humanitarian aid and the convoys could have been different if the enclave was totally demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I -- had the UN completely demilitarised the Srebrenica enclave, and by extension the Zepa enclave, I suspect that the VRS would have factored that into their calculations as to the issue of humanitarian aid. If they were comfortable with the fact that none of the aid that would have been going in could have had a potential military use, you know, it may very well have impacted their decision to allow that aid in.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to look at page 4 of this same document, right at the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Right at the bottom of page 4, in the last part of this paragraph, what we see is: [In English] "The government actions are designed in part to convince the International Community that the cessation of hostilities agreement is not working, with the aim of discrediting the Bosnian Serbs. In fact, it is the Bosnian government which is proving the more difficult by imposing new restrictions on freedom of movement and refusing to attend joint commission meetings." [Interpretation] Do you agree that the constant behaviour of the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in particular in 1995, demonstrate that they intend to compromise any agreement with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's calling for speculation, and it's massively broad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau. Do you wish to proceed with your next question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know the route taken by the convoys when they went to Karakaj to go to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am. My understanding is that most of the convoys that -- that were going there went in and out of the international border crossings along the Drina. You know, there may have been a few that went in through Karakaj, but I think the bulk of them went in through the border crossings of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that when convoys entered from Yugoslavia into Bosnia-Herzegovina to go to Srebrenica, they didn't go through Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I would assume that convoys entering at Zvornik and taking the road south to Srebrenica would have to, at some juncture, pass through Konjevic Polje. Certainly, the convoys entering at the Loznica -- I'm sorry, not Loznica, but Ljubovo-Bratunac area would not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You analysed a series of documents from the staff, in particular those relating to convoys. Would you agree to say that the name of General Milovanovic appears on many of these documents right up to the end of May 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, his name does appear on a number of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show the witness P2891. It is an OTP document that is only in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is an order from the Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska on the 28th of April, 1995. I'm going to read out the first paragraph, item 1: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not receiving -- madam, we are not receiving the interpretation in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, yeah. I think you can proceed now again. You have to start again, madame, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Still not getting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We still have a problem. We're not getting the interpretation. I would wait for a while, but we never got it. So what's the problem? Shall we try again? Sorry, Madame Fauveau. I mean, it's not your fault at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No matter. " ... With a view to combining the activities of the forces engaged according to the Fletcher Plan 95 and a more efficient implementation of the orders issued and the creation of conditions for the realisation of the operation Coordinated Action 1995, I hereby issue the following order: From the Main Staff officers of the VRS, led by the chief of staff, set up the forward command post 1 in Zvornik at the former forward command post of the Drina Corps, and the forward command post 2 in Bijeljina, at the command post of the Eastern Bosnian Corps." For the time being, can you tell me whether these are the operations that were mentioned in directive 7 and 7-1?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, and those have to do with -- you know, in the context of time, what is happening here is less an offensive operation but more the fact that the ABiH 2 Corps has initiated its large offensive against Mount Majevica and that what is happening here is that the VRS is having to react to that with the forces of the northern component of the Drina Corps and of the East Bosnia Corps to defend that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to this document, the chief of the -- the chief of staff was the one in charge of setting up the post at Zvornik. We're talking about General Milovanovic, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic is, by formation, the chief of staff, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you drafted your report on the responsibility of members of the staff, did you take into account that at the end of April 1995, General Milovanovic is in charge of setting up forward command post at Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I did not. I'm not exactly sure how it's particularly relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show the witness 5D714. What I think is relevant is item 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We're still here talking about the Spreca 1995 operation, and let me read out to you paragraph 1 and 2(a): "From among the officers of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, three teams are to be set up to be engaged in providing assistance, combining combat activities, and ascertaining the state of affairs in the 1st Bratunac Brigade or Birac Brigade. In accordance with the order of the president of Republika Srpska, the composition of the first team, the first team, Lieutenant Colonel General Milovanovic, Manojlo Milovanovic." My question is this: On the 12th of May, 1995, do you know that General Milovanovic went into the field in the Drina Corps area to examine combat activities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I did not specifically know that at this date.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, but according to this document, General Milovanovic, as the chief of staff, would go into the field in order to monitor the situation in the field, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. While normally the chief of staff is the stay-home person, while the commander or other members of the operation staff do that, you know, the fact that the chief of staff does do it is not remarkable. It's a perfectly normal occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to show you Exhibit P2669A, and be reassured that there is a translation -- an English translation of this document, and I believe that you've already seen this document. It's an order from the staff regarding the deployment of UNPROFOR prisoners, and this document is dated 27th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Before going into this document, let me remind you that on the 16th of January, at page 19764, you mentioned that order and you stated that item 5 of this order dealt with prisoners -- people taken prisoners at the Echo post. I'd like to show you page 2 of this document in English for you to be able to read item 5. In B/C/S, it's also page 2 of the document. When you read item 5 of this document, you see that the Command of the SRK has to disarm the remaining blocked UNPROFOR forces. Would you agree that the Command of the SRK here is the Command of the Sarajevo Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Then they're supposed to disarm the remaining forces and to deploy them to various installations, pursuant to item 1 of the order. Could we go back to item 1 of the document, please, on page 1 of the document. At point 1, all corps are mentioned, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I take that to mean all the major formations, which were the 6 Corps commands as well as the air-and-air forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And therefore the first wave of captured UNPROFOR personnel were deployed in the Krajina Corps area, the Eastern Bosnia Corps and the Bosnia and Herzegovina Corps area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to page 2 of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At paragraph 5, mention is made of UNPROFOR forces that have to be disarmed by the Command of the Sarajevo Corps and that they have to be deployed in the Drina Corps area of responsibility. Isn't that what we understand when reading the second page of this paragraph? Sorry, the second sentence of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am. I take it that -- I take it from this paragraph that the Command of the Drina Corps will take any captured UNPROFOR troops or members of the International Community that it takes, not that they're going to await for additional people from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, but according to you, the second group -- the second wave of people that have to be disarmed by the SRK, where should they be deployed, this second group of people?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the first sentence, it's to deploy them at installations pursuant to paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And item 1 refers to all the corps. Why not to the Drina Corps, then?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the Drina Corps did not have any UN individuals under its custody, I presume. And that's why, like I said, when I read the second sentence of paragraph 5, the way I read it is that, you know, once the Drina Corps does get such people into their custody, it will place them in installations within its area of responsibility. I do not take -- because it's two separate sentences, I do not take paragraph 5 as an interpretation that it's the responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps to take additional UN -- UNPROFOR people and turn them over to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: According to this order, no order is given to the Command of the Drina Corps to capture UNPROFOR personnel, and the Command of the SRK is supposed to disarm these people and to deploy them in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, there's no -- there's no -- there's no explicit instruction for the Command of the Drina Corps to actually capture any of these individuals. I take it that that's the inference behind this.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me correct page 36, line 1. I did not mention the 3rd Corps. I mentioned the other formations, the other corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Earlier on, at page 35, line 15 and 16 of the transcript, you stated that at the time the Drina Corps -- or you believe that at the time the Drina Corps did not have any UNPROFOR members in its custody. When you say that you think or you suppose, it means that you're not sure of your fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am. As far as I'm aware, at that particular time the Drina Corps had not specifically captured or been able to detain any UN members. So as I noted in my earlier response to the Office of the Prosecutor, or the Prosecutor's question on that, you know, they were also aware that they were going to begin military operations against the UN forces with respect to Observation Post Echo. So I take this is to be that, you know, if UN people should come into their custody as part of that, this is what the Drina Corps is supposed to do, is supposed to deploy them in accordance with the previous instructions in installations around the corps zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Don't you believe, sir, that you're speculating when you are making that statement, because that's nowhere to be found in this order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I agree. As I told you before, it's not -- it's not explicitly stated that the Command of the Drina Corps will capture those -- will capture individuals. I believe that it is inferred behind the intent here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This order is dated 27th of May, 1995, and the name we find here is that of General Milovanovic. Would you agree that at the end of May 1995, and we saw that it was the case also in April and on the 12th of May, 1995, would you agree that General Milovanovic did not only deal with Western Bosnia, he also dealt with affairs pertaining to the Drina Corps and the Sarajevo Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ma'am, as evidenced by this particular document, he dealt with the affairs of the entire army. Particularly of note is his listing is not even as chief of staff in this context, it's as deputy commander, implying that General Mladic, for whatever reason, is unavailable to issue this order and it's being issued under the authority of General Milovanovic as his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that General Milovanovic, when he was at the forward command post, was acting as the deputy commander of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In times of absence by General Mladic, you know, General Milovanovic would have been, you know, in a de jure role the deputy commander of the VRS, yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that General Milovanovic, as the chief of staff, was the deputy commander of General Mladic because of the establishment, he did not need to receive any particular order to fulfill that these -- position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I agree. I mean, the inherent authorities that he had as the chief of staff of the Main Staff and as deputy commander meant that he did not need any specific order to function in that role when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that General Mladic [as interpreted], as chief of operations and training, was not, as such -- because of his position, was not, as such, the deputy commander -- or the deputy chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, ma'am, I disagree. By -- by position, the chief of operations is the deputy chief of staff and functions as such when the chief of staff is unavailable or, you know, otherwise cannot perform the role. I mean, in the same way that General Milovanovic is the deputy commander under those same circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Let me correct page 38, line 3 of the transcript. I'm talking about General Miletic and not General Mladic? On what basis did you come to that conclusion? I'm talking about the answer you've just given me.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ma'am, as the -- looking at the JNA command and staff regulations of 1983, 1984, looking at the corps regulations, looking at the relevant brigade regulations, all of them are consistent with designating that the chief of operations has the responsibility, as the deputy chief of staff of a formation, in the absence of the chief of staff. So, you know, given the fact that the Main Staff is functionally organised along the same criteria, for the most part, that the corps are, my view is that, and I believe others have verified, that the chief of operations of the Main Staff, you know, does in fact assume the position of deputy chief of staff in the absence of the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Would you agree that the rules you've analysed are the rules that apply at a lower level, at the brigade level and the corps level, but they -- we're not talking about rules that apply specifically to the staff, the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: To the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, ma'am. We don't have a set of instructions for how the Main Staff is organised. A main staff is not a body that's formed under regulations, at least not as far as I'm aware, so in that context what it did was -- I had to take the lower-level rules and then to determine whether or not those same rules and practices were applicable to the Main Staff. And one of those was whether or not the chief of operations had a concurrent role as the deputy chief of staff. And again as part of the investigative process, that is one of the questions that we'd asked a number of individuals who were on the Main Staff, as to whether or not that was in effect, and the answer that we got was an affirmative, that, you know, they acknowledge that, you know, their understanding, as members of that body, was that, you know, in the absence of the chief of staff, General Miletic, as the chief of operations, assumed that role.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you ever come across an official document from the VRS related to the structure of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, and in that regard I think the most useful document that I came across was the 1992 analysis of the combat operations of the VRS, because inherent in that document, which lays out all of the combat roles and functions of the VRS, the report was authored in part by the Main Staff, and in each particular segment of that report you get an understanding about what the Main Staff's roles and functions were into overseeing those activities. So you can actually do a fairly good job of taking that report and using that to organise the structure of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'll come back to that document later, but now I'd like to show you document 5D431. Have you ever seen this document? It's a portion of the document. Could we zoom in on the part of the document in English, where it says "Establishment number."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I've seen this document in the last several months. I don't believe that I had this document when I was doing my reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we display the third page of this document, page 3, please. Page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You see right at the bottom of this page, fourth line, we can see: [In English] "Chief of staff, deputy commander."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then afterwards you see: [In English] "Chief." [Interpretation] And here there's no mention that this person is also the deputy chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, that's correct, there's no mention of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Here we see the "Operations Department." That's part of the Operations and Training Administration. And here again we have the chief, who is at the same time the deputy head of ONP Administration. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. When -- it's normally the operations person, in the absence of the chief of operations, it's the head operations person who assumes the role as the deputy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Based on this establishment, based on this formation, could we agree that it's not the head of the ONP Administration who is the chief of staff when the chief of staff is not present?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ma'am, as I noted, it doesn't say that. However, the information that I'm aware of reflects the fact that the head of -- that the head of ONP did function as the deputy chief of staff. So, I mean, I understand that particular document doesn't say that. However, I believe that the large body of information, much of it that has come before here reflecting him perform the duties, you know, as essentially the chief of staff, runs counter to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You've been shown or you've seen a great deal of documents signed by General Miletic, who was first a colonel, with the mention "zastupa" in B/C/S, [B/C/S spoken], and in most cases this was translated by standing in for the chief of staff. Did you notice that in some document, this "zastupa," this mention "zastupa" was translated by chief of staff representative, [In English] "and also on behalf of chief of staff"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that there are different translations with respect to standing in for the chief of staff or standing in for another officer or a -- there's a lesser abbreviation just known as "za" where the individual is signing for that person. My understanding is that with respect to -- with respect to the formalised title that we're doing is when the person has signed it that way or is titled as standing in for the chief of staff or standing in for a particular individual, that it's a more formalised process than somebody just signing for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you ever ask the translators to explain this difference in the translation in English of this phrase?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, and where it first came up was in the analysis of Zvornik Brigade documents that we saw in August and September of 1995, where we noticed a particular phrase associated with Major Dragan Obrenovic standing in for the commander. And in that context, what I asked the translators to do was to go back to the JNA military lexicon, which gives those definitions, so I could understand what that particular phrase meant in context of command authority, what it entitled the commander or what it entitled an individual to do or to not do. So, I mean, that's -- I was aware, when that particular issue came up, that there was a difference in terminology that I had to explore.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But did anybody ever tell you that in B/C/S, "zastupa" can have different meanings and refer to the various levels of standing in for someone or representing someone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I went to the JNA military lexicon, because military terminology by and large is designed to be clear so there is absolutely no confusion, on a battlefield environment, as to what it means and what the phrase -- you know, what the phrase implies and what it means in the military sense. So that's why we went to that particular reference source, to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This lexicon dates back to the year 1981, if I'm not mistaken. Are you aware that after the war started, a number of words started meaning something different, started changing, depending on the state or on the territory they were used?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ma'am, I will assume that that's the case. But having said that, my understanding is, again going back to the JNA military lexicon, and of course, you know, these were questions that we asked VRS officers as we started gaining access to them, to ask them what these particular phrases meant as well, if there was any confusion. So, you know, in my mind there's not any confusion behind it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned Obrenovic. Isn't it the case that Obrenovic was not standing in for but was the acting commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- and, again, it may be a linguistic and terminology issue, but the phrase that we associate with Obrenovic is "the acting commander," because in a command sense, you know, somebody standing in for the commander does not have inherently the same legal authorities that an individual would do if he were acting as that particular person. My understanding is in the case of Obrenovic, while I know that sometimes the translations go one way or another, the actual term of art we used during that period for him is that he's acting -- he's the acting commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General Milovanovic was chief of staff of the VRS. He was the direct superior of General Miletic. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On Friday, not last Friday but the Friday before that, at page 20009, you said that Obrenovic, who was standing in for the commander whilst [indiscernible] was not there, only had the authority to deal with daily matters, daily affairs. Isn't it the case that General Miletic, when General Milovanovic was not there, could only deal with daily matters, daily affairs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I don't believe that, even though General Milovanovic was present at an IKM or in Banja Luka or another location, General Miletic had the authority to essentially perform as General Milovanovic would. General Miletic, you know, in assuming the position as the deputy chief of staff, you know, is going to act within the competence of his position and in light of the guidance that he receives from General Milovanovic and General Mladic in that manner. Again, any authority that he is performing under, you know, has been delegated by General Milovanovic in that respect. It is not an independent authority that he has.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that General Miletic never performed the full range of functions of General Milovanovic, the same that the latter performed; would you agree to say that General Milovanovic took part in the meetings with the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- while I don't have a whole documentary basis to say that, I'm fairly comfortable saying that certainly General Miletic, you know, would not have performed the entire range of functions that General Milovanovic was entitled to perform based on his position.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We all saw that General Milovanovic went into the field in May to monitor the situation. From what you know, in 1995, did General Miletic go there? He didn't, did he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether or not General Miletic at any point left the Main Staff headquarters facility to go out and monitor anything in the field. I have no information one way or another on that, so I don't know that I can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 15th of January, 1995, you talked about an order dated the 1st of May, 1993, and the order which was drafted by General Miletic and signed by General Milovanovic. Well, you said that at the time General Miletic was a deputy of Colonel Ilic, who was the chief of the operations for education at the time. What is the source of your information, when you say that on the 1st of May, 1993, General Miletic was the deputy of the -- of Colonel Ilic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that the -- there is a document which lists, in some respect in a similar manner to this, it lists the formations and positions of the individuals assigned to the Main Staff during the course of the war. That particular document, and again I don't know the number of it offhand, has a penciled-in notation on Colonel Miletic showing at what point in time he was -- he was a member of various organs of the Main Staff. It's that particular document which I base my information off of. And, again, while I don't recall what number it would be offhand, I think I have a copy of it among my notes somewhere, and it's something I can produce, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that you do not know what the exact function of General Miletic was in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm basing my understanding of the function of then Colonel Miletic off of that particular document. It says what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you agree that the administrative operations and training of the Main Staff was made up of the -- [Technical difficulties] -- Operations department and the department for training and the department premises -- the operations premises? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
